---
title: "Status and Prestige in Two-Mode Networks"
---

## Two-Mode Networks as Prisms

We can use the same "prismatic" mode of status distribution to rank nodes in two-mode networks that we used in the [standard one-mode case](prest-eigen.qmd). The difference is that in the one-mode case you gain status by connecting to entities of the same "type" as you (e.g., other people); but in the two-mode case, your status reflects the status of the *other type* entities that you connect to. And vice versa. 

For instance, if the two entities are persons and groups as in the classic case [@breiger74], then people gain status by connecting to high-status groups and groups gain status by connecting to high-status people. In other words, people distribute status points to the groups they belong to, and groups distribute status points they got from those people back to the people who chose them. 

When it comes to **eigenvector**-style measures (see [here](basic-eigen.qmd)), the neat idea is that *people are central if they belong to central groups and groups are central if their members are central people*, with people centrality defined by membership in central groups can be effectively captured by these metrics [@bonacich91].

For this reason, measures of status and prestige are particularly applicable to two-mode networks. This is because the *reflective* principle behind these measures interacts well with the *duality* principle. 

## Two-Mode Bonacich Prestige 

Let's see an example using the classic Southern Women dataset. We can load it from the trusty `networkdata` package, and extract the bi-adjacency matrix from the `igraph` object:

```{r}
library(networkdata)
library(igraph)
g <- southern_women
A <- as.matrix(as_biadjacency_matrix(g))
```

Below is a quick function that plays a two-mode version of the status distribution game that we described in the [status and prestige lesson](prest-eigen.qmd), and which is really just a modification of the one-mode HITS algorithm due to @kleinberg99:

```{r}
tm.status <- function(w, z) {
  y <- matrix(1 / ncol(w), ncol(w), 1) # initial group status column vector set to a constant
  delta <- 1
  k <- 0
  while (delta > 1e-10) {
    o.y <- y # old group status scores
    x <- w %*% o.y # new people scores a function of people matrix and old group scores
    x <- x / norm(x, type = "F") # normalizing new people status scores
    y <- z %*% x # new group scores a function of group matrix and new people scores
    y <- y / norm(y, type = "F") # normalizing new group status scores
    delta <- max(abs(y - o.y)) # max element-wise change in group status scores
    k <- k + 1
  }
  return(list(p.s = x, g.s = y))
}
```

The function takes the two-mode **biadjacency matrix** $\mathbf{A}$ and its **transpose** $\mathbf{A}^T$ as input and returns a vector of row-mode nodes (e.g., persons) scores `p.s`, a vector of column-mode (e.g., groups) status scores `g.s`.

The function works like this:

- Line 2 initializes the original status scores for each group stored in the `y` object, which are just set to $|G|^{-1}$, where $|G|$ is the number of groups (the number of columns of the bi-adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$). 
- Line 3 initializes the $\delta$ value, which determines when the `while` loop stops. Then, inside the `while` loop starting on line 5, we assign status scores to the people equal to the sum of the status scores of the groups they belong to in line 7, which is just $\mathbf{A}$ (`w`) post-multiplied by the group status vector $\mathbf{y}$; then we normalize the people status score vector in line 8 using the Euclidean vector norm. 
- In line 9 we calculate the new group status vector (`y`), which, for each group, is given by the sum of the status scores of the people that belong to it that we computed in line 7 (the transpose of the matrix `z` post-multiplied by the vector `x`). 
- Finally, we normalize the new group status scores in line 10 and compute the difference between these new group scores and the old one to calculate $\delta$. When $\delta$ is small ($\delta \leq 10^{-10}$) the `while` loop stops as the old and new scores have achieved convergence.

We can now use the `tm.status` function to estimate the status scores for people and groups:

```{r}
tm.hits <- tm.status(A, t(A))
```

Here are the scores for the people:

```{r}
round(tm.hits$p.s / max(tm.hits$p.s), 3)
```

And for the groups:

```{r}
round(tm.hits$g.s / max(tm.hits$g.s), 3)
```

Here, `Theresa` is the top person (attending the most central events), closely followed by `Evelyn`, with `Flora` and `Nora` toward the bottom. The event held on 9/16 is the top event (attended by the most central people).

When we use the usual affiliation matrix `A` and its transpose `t(A)` as inputs, the `tm.status` function implements the biHITS algorithm described in @liao_etal14. Note that the biHITS algorithm is essentially a rediscovery of the two-mode prestige scoring described earlier by @bonacich91. 

### The Dual Projection Approach

As @bonacich91 noted in that paper, the eigenvector status scores can also be obtained by playing the one-mode version of the status game over the Breiger-style one-mode projections of the two-mode network. 

To see this, let's bring back the `status1` function we wrote before for the one-mode case:

```{r}
status1 <- function(w) {
  x <- rep(1, nrow(w)) # initial status vector set to all ones of length equal to the number of nodes
  d <- 1 # initial delta
  k <- 0 # initializing counter
  while (d > 1e-10) {
    o.x <- x # old status scores
    x <- w %*% o.x # new scores a function of old scores and adjacency matrix
    x <- x / norm(x, type = "F") # normalizing new status scores
    d <- max(abs(x - o.x)) # max element-wise difference between new and old scores
    k <- k + 1 # incrementing while counter
  }
  return(as.vector(x))
}
```

And now, let's play the usual status game defined by the function `status1` over the one-mode projections `P` and `G`. For people, this would be:

```{r}
P <- A %*% t(A)
p.s <- status1(P)
names(p.s) <- rownames(A)
round(p.s / max(p.s), 3)
```

And for groups:

```{r}
G <- t(A) %*% A
g.s <- status1(G)
names(g.s) <- colnames(A)
round(g.s / max(g.s), 3)
```

Lo and behold, these are the same status scores we obtained via the biHITS approach. 

### The Eigenvector Approach

Of course, these scores are usually called two-mode "Eigenvector Centralities" because they can be obtained by solving the linear equation system:

$$
\lambda \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}
$$

$$
\lambda \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{x}
$$

This says that the status scores of persons $\mathbf{x}$ are just the sums of the status scores of the groups each person is connected to, and the status scores of groups $\mathbf{y}$ are just the sum of the scores of the people that join them. 

As we saw in the discussion of [prestige scoring for one-mode networks](prest-eigen.qmd), this is the usual cat-chasing-its-own-tail circular equation problem. To figure out the person status scores $\mathbf{x}$, we need the group status scores $\mathbf{y}$, and vice versa.

This is also a classic eigenvector/eigenvalue problem, so we can find the person and group status scores using the [eigendecomposition](prest-eigen.qmd) approach.

Since we have a rectangular biadjacency matrix, we can proceed in two ways. We can obtain the eigenvector/eigenvalue pairs via **singular value decomposition** of the biadjacency matrix itself, or via standard eigendecomposition of each of its projections separately. 

Let's see the first approach in action first, using the `R` function `svd`:

```{r}
eig <- svd(A) # singular value decomposition of biadjacency matrix
# SVD/eigenvector signs are arbitrary: standardize by flipping so the largest-magnitude element is positive
std.sign <- function(v) v * sign(v[which.max(abs(v))])
eig.p <- std.sign(eig$u[, 1]) # vector of person prestige scores
eig.g <- std.sign(eig$v[, 1]) # vector of group prestige scores
names(eig.p) <- rownames(A)
names(eig.g) <- colnames(A)
```

And for the big reveal:

```{r}
round(eig.p / max(eig.p), 3)
round(eig.g / max(eig.g), 3)
```

As you can see, these are the same scores we obtained earlier. 

For the second approach the person and group prestige scores can be computed by figuring out the leading eigenvector of the @breiger74 projection matrices:

$$
\lambda \mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T)\mathbf{x}
$$

$$
\lambda \mathbf{y} = (\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})\mathbf{y}
$$

In `R` we can do this using the `eigen` function:

```{r}
eig.p <- eigen(P)
eig.g <- eigen(G)
p.s <- std.sign(eig.p$vector[, 1])
g.s <- std.sign(eig.g$vector[, 1])
names(p.s) <- rownames(A)
names(g.s) <- colnames(A)
```

And for the big reveal:

```{r}
round(p.s / max(p.s), 3)
round(g.s / max(g.s), 3)
```

Neat! These are the same scores we obtained by playing our status game on the affiliation matrix (biHITS) using `tm.status`, playing the same game on the one-mode projection (Bonacich) using the `status1` function, or using `svd` to obtain the leading eigenvector of the biadjacency matrix. 

The scores are also readily interpretable: The most central people belong to the most central (largest membership) groups and the most central groups are the ones that attract the most central (highest activity) members. 

### The Duality of Bonacich Prestige

Another way of thinking of the eigenvector status score of each node in this context is as a weighted sum of the eigenvector centralities on the nodes in the other mode they are connected to [@faust97, p. 170].^[Where the weight is the inverse of the square root of the first eigenvalue obtained from the `eigen` analysis. The square root is not so mysterious: the nonzero eigenvalues of the projection matrices $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^T$ and $\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ are the squares of those of the coupled two-mode system, so the eigenvalue $\lambda$ linking the two modes is the square root of the projections' leading eigenvalue.] 

For instance, the unnormalized eigenvector status scores for persons and groups are:

```{r}
p.s
g.s
```

So for any person, let's say `Evelyn`, their eigenvector centrality is equal to:

```{r}
sum(A["EVELYN", ] * g.s) * 1 / sqrt(eig.p$values[1])
```

Which is indeed `Evelyn`'s Eigenvector score.

The same goes for the eigenvector score of groups, which are just a weighted sum of the Eigenvector centralities of the people who belong to them:

```{r}
sum(A[, "6/27"] * p.s) * 1 / sqrt(eig.p$values[1])
```

Which is indeed the eigenvector score for the event held on `6-27`. 

Duality at work!

## Two-Mode PageRank

Like in the case of the usual eigenvector approach to calculating status, the distribution game in the function `tm.status` assumes that persons and groups distribute the same amount of status regardless of their own degree (which you recall for people is the number of memberships and for groups is the number of members). 

But just like with regular PageRank for one-mode networks, we can change this assumption in the two-mode case by presuming that people get more status points to distribute when they belong to exclusive (smaller) groups, and groups get more status to distribute when their members are more selective in their affiliation behavior (they have a smaller number of memberships).

To do that, we create new versions of the affiliation matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and its transpose $\mathbf{A}^T$ normalized by the group and person degrees (respectively). 

To do this, imagine $\mathbf{D}_p$ as a diagonal matrix containing the *inverse* of each person's degree (number of memberships). This matrix can be created in `R` using the following quick function:

```{r}
inv.deg <- function(k, pow = 1) {
  if (any(k == 0)) {
    stop("Isolated nodes present: remove them or handle them explicitly before normalizing.")
  }
  diag(1 / k^pow)
}
D.p <- inv.deg(rowSums(A))
round(D.p, 2)
```

Recalling that, as we discussed earlier in the basic two-mode statistics lesson, the row sums of $\mathbf{A}$ give us the person degrees.^[Note the guard in the helper function `inv.deg` because PageRank-style scoring divides by the degrees; it is undefined for nodes with zero ties (isolates), and including them would silently propagate infinite values through the iteration. The function therefore stops with an informative error rather than proceeding; the fully general solution is the damped version of the algorithm, which adds a teleportation step so zero-degree nodes retain their prior score. For large bipartite networks, it is also worth building the diagonal matrices sparsely with `Matrix::Diagonal(x = 1 / k^pow)` rather than densely, since the dense version is mostly zeros.]

We do the same for groups by creating a matrix $\mathbf{D}_g$ containing the *inverse* of each group's degree (number of members) along the diagonal.

```{r}
D.g <- inv.deg(colSums(A))
round(D.g, 2)
```

Recalling that the column sums of $\mathbf{A}$ give us the group degrees.

Now we can construct degree-normalized versions of the original bi-adjacency matrix and its transpose like this:

```{r}
P.n <- A %*% D.g
colnames(P.n) <- colnames(A)
G.n <- t(A) %*% D.p
colnames(G.n) <- rownames(A)
```

Let's see what's in the matrix `P.n`:

```{r}
round(P.n, 2)
```

The `P.n` matrix is of the same dimensions as the original affiliation matrix `A`. However, the ${ij}^{th}$ cell is now $1/k_j$, where $k_j$ is the number of members in group $j$. That means that if group $j$ has a lot of members, then the ${ij}^{th}$ cell will contain a small number (as in the non-zero entries in the column corresponding to event `9-16`) but when the group is small, the ${ij}^{th}$ cell will contain a bigger number (as in the non-zero entries in the column corresponding to event `11-21`). This means people in smaller groups will have more centrality points to distribute. 

The same goes for groups, as we can see by checking out the `G.n` matrix:

```{r}
round(G.n, 2)
```

Note that both matrices `P.n` and `G.n` are **column stochastic**, which means that their columns sum to one. We can check for this property as follows:

```{r}
colSums(P.n)
colSums(G.n)
```

So now, to calculate the two-mode PageRank status score, we just play our two-mode status game on these matrices: 

```{r}
tm.pr <- tm.status(P.n, G.n)
```

Note that because the bi-adjacency matrices that go into the `tm.status` function are already normalized, the additional Euclidean normalization inside the function is redundant: it only rescales the score vectors by a constant, leaving the rankings unchanged.

Here are the resulting scores for the people:

```{r}
round(tm.pr$p.s / max(tm.pr$p.s), 3)
```

And for the groups:

```{r}
round(tm.pr$g.s / max(tm.pr$g.s), 3)
```

The resulting scores match those returned by the "co-HITS" algorithm in @deng_etal09. 

In this ranking, the top persons are `Theresa` and `Nora` (who wasn't as highly ranked according to the Bonacich prestige), and `Dorothy`, `Olivia`, and `Flora` are the least prestigious. The top-ranked event took place on `9-16`. 

We can of course obtain the same two-mode PageRank scores using different approaches. One alternative is to use the "PageRank" projections and play the regular (one-mode) status game on them:

```{r}
P.pr <- P.n %*% G.n
G.pr <- G.n %*% P.n
pr.p <- status1(P.pr)
pr.g <- status1(G.pr)
names(pr.p) <- rownames(A)
names(pr.g) <- colnames(A)
round(pr.p / max(pr.p), 3)
round(pr.g / max(pr.g), 3)
```

Neat!

Yet another approach is to compute the leading eigenvector of the PageRank normalized projections using the `eigen` function, which is the same as playing the `status1` game on them:

```{r}
pr.p <- abs(Re(eigen(P.pr)$vectors[, 1]))
names(pr.p) <- rownames(A)
round(pr.p / max(pr.p), 3)

pr.g <- abs(Re(eigen(G.pr)$vectors[, 1]))
names(pr.g) <- colnames(A)
round(pr.g / max(pr.g), 3)
```

Which gives us the same solutions as before. 

## Double Normalized Two-Mode PageRank

Recall that the main reason for using PageRank normalization in the two-mode case (and preferring PageRank scoring over eigenvector scoring) is to give more status points to discerning people, so people in more exclusive clubs distribute more centrality in the system. So, to do that, we divided each person's centrality points according to the size of the group they belong to, so that `Evelyn` gets 0.33 centrality points for attending event 6/27 because that event was attended by only three people, which is more than she gets for attending event 4/8, which was attended by twelve people (and the same for events).

However, PageRank centrality rankings can still be affected by the sheer *number* of events a person attends (or the sheer number of members of a group) even if that person is not particularly selective. Thus, a person who attends many not-very-selective (well-attended) events still contributes as much centrality to the system as someone who attends fewer but more selective events. It would be nice if a PageRank-style score could account for both the selectivity of the events attended and the number of events attended, so a person who attends many not-very-selective events doesn't get an advantage over someone who attends fewer but more selective events.

To do that, it would be useful to come up with versions of `P.n` and `G.n` that normalize (for persons) by the exclusivity of the groups they attend *and* by the number of events they go to, so as not to give an advantage to those who attend a lot of events. Similarly, it would be useful to normalize (for groups) by the discernment of their members *and* by the number of members they have, so as not to give an advantage to well-attended events.

For people, we can proceed as follows:

```{r}
P.n2 <- D.p %*% A %*% D.g
rownames(P.n2) <- rownames(A)
colnames(P.n2) <- colnames(A)
```

Let's see what's inside the new `P.n2` matrix:

```{r}
round(P.n2, 2)
```

We can see that people with lots of memberships (like `Evelyn`) get their centrality points reduced relative to people with fewer memberships, like `Charlotte`. 

This is easy to see if we compare the row sums of the two matrices, which give us the total amount of centrality points each person has to distribute:

```{r}
rowSums(P.n)
rowSums(P.n2)
```

Note that while in the original `P.n` matrix `Evelyn` has way more centrality points to distribute than `Charlotte` (a ratio of `r round(rowSums(P.n)[1]/rowSums(P.n)[5], 2)`), this discrepancy is much smaller in the new `P.n2` double-normalized matrix (a ratio of `r round(rowSums(P.n2)[1]/rowSums(P.n2)[5], 2)`). 

We can now the same normalization for groups:

```{r}
G.n2 <- D.g %*% t(A) %*% D.p
rownames(G.n2) <- colnames(A)
colnames(G.n2) <- rownames(A)
```


Now to compute our double-normalized PageRank status scores, we just play the status game on these degree-normalized matrices:

```{r}
tm.bgrm <- tm.status(P.n2, G.n2)
```
Which implements the "BGRM" algorithm of @rui_etal07 [589, eq. 8].^[The acronym stands for "Bipartite Graph Reinforcement Model."] 

Here are the resulting scores for the people:

```{r}
round(tm.bgrm$p.s / max(tm.bgrm$p.s), 3)
```

And for the groups:

```{r}
round(tm.bgrm$g.s / max(tm.bgrm$g.s), 3)
```

We can see that the highest-ranked women are now `Olivia` and `Flora` (compared with `Evelyn`, `Theresa`, and `Nora` in the standard PageRank scores), who used to rank near the bottom under traditional Bonacich prestige or PageRank scoring. Similarly, the top event is now the one held on 2/23, which wasn't particularly distinguished by the other ranking algorithms. 

@he_etal16 provide a small twist on the double-normalized approach. They suggest that rather than normalizing the adjacency by the inverse of the degrees of each node, we should use the *square root* of the degrees. They call their approach "Birank". 

Here's how it works. First, we create our new $\mathbf{P}$ matrix for people:

```{r}
P.n3 <- inv.deg(rowSums(A), pow = 1 / 2) %*% A %*% inv.deg(colSums(A), pow = 1 / 2)
rownames(P.n3) <- rownames(A)
colnames(P.n3) <- colnames(A)
```

And another for the groups:

```{r}
G.n3 <- inv.deg(colSums(A), pow = 1 / 2) %*% t(A) %*% inv.deg(rowSums(A), pow = 1 / 2)
rownames(G.n3) <- colnames(A)
colnames(G.n3) <- rownames(A)
```

And now we run our status game on these matrices:

```{r}
tm.birank <- tm.status(P.n3, G.n3)
```

And here are the resulting scores for people:

```{r}
round(tm.birank$p.s / max(tm.birank$p.s), 3)
```

And for the groups:

```{r}
round(tm.birank$g.s / max(tm.birank$g.s), 3)
```

A summary of the four prestige ranking models for two-mode networks goes as follows:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-tmranks
#| tbl-cap: "Prestige Scores for the Southern Women Data According to Four Algorithms"
#| tbl-subcap:
#| - "Persons"
#| - "Groups"
#| layout-ncol: 2

p.tab <- data.frame(
  hits = round(tm.hits$p.s / max(tm.hits$p.s), 3),
  pr = round(tm.pr$p.s / max(tm.pr$p.s), 3),
  bgrm = round(tm.bgrm$p.s / max(tm.bgrm$p.s), 3),
  birank = round(tm.birank$p.s / max(tm.birank$p.s), 3),
  k = rowSums(A)
)
p.tab <- p.tab[order(p.tab$k, decreasing = TRUE), ]
g.tab <- data.frame(
  hits = round(tm.hits$g.s / max(tm.hits$g.s), 3),
  pr = round(tm.pr$g.s / max(tm.pr$g.s), 3),
  bgrm = round(tm.bgrm$g.s / max(tm.bgrm$g.s), 3),
  birank = round(tm.birank$g.s / max(tm.birank$g.s), 3),
  k = colSums(A)
)
g.tab <- g.tab[order(g.tab$k, decreasing = TRUE), ]
library(kableExtra)
kbl(p.tab,
  format = "html", align = "c",
  caption = "Person Prestige Scores Ordered by Degree"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("hover", "condensed", "responsive")) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
kbl(g.tab,
  format = "html", align = "c",
  caption = "Group Prestige Scores Ordered by Degree"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("hover", "condensed", "responsive")) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE)
```

## Mapping to the BiRank Package

The four algorithms described in this lecture are implemented, under their more standard names, in the `birankr` (R) and `birankpy` (Python) packages, which unify them as special cases of a single coupled PageRank-style iteration over the bipartite network @yang_etal20. The table below maps each model in this note to its package name and original source.^[One technical difference is worth noting: the package's update equations include damping factors $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (set to 0.85) and prior score vectors, which add a teleportation step to the iteration. The `tm.status` function above runs the pure (undamped) power-method version of each algorithm, so the scores converge to the dominant eigenvector pair of the corresponding transition matrices without the smoothing induced by damping.]

|Model in This Note|Matrices Passed to `tm.status`|`birankr`/`birankpy` Method|Source|
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
|Two-Mode Bonacich Prestige (biHITS)|`A`, `t(A)` (raw biadjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A}^T$)|HITS|@kleinberg99; @liao_etal14, both equivalent to @bonacich91|
|Two-Mode PageRank|`P.n` = $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_g$; `G.n` = $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{D}_p$|CoHITS|@deng_etal09|
|Double-Normalized Two-Mode PageRank|`P.n2` = $\mathbf{D}_p\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}_g$; `G.n2` = $\mathbf{D}_g\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{D}_p$|BGRM|@rui_etal07|
|Square-Root Double Normalization|`P.n3` = $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_p\mathbf{A}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_g$; `G.n3` = $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_g\mathbf{A}^T\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_p$, where $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}$ contains the inverse square-root degrees|BiRank|@he_etal16|

: The four two-mode prestige algorithms in this note and their counterparts in the BiRank package {#tbl-birankmap}
